units.title: Unit 01 — What is a collocation?
learningObjectives: Recognise natural word combinations across several grammatical patterns.
Distinguish lexical combinations that sound natural from literal but unnatural alternatives.
Choose idiomatic partners and register-sensitive alternatives in original contexts.

items.example: Her blond hair looked almost silver in the morning light.
items.note: For natural hair colour descriptions, blond is preferred to yellow.

items.example: The unexpected results aroused interest among the researchers.
items.note: Use arouse with interest, curiosity or suspicion to describe causing a response.

items.example: Dr Patel will lead a seminar on scientific communication.
items.note: Lead a seminar is natural for the person guiding the discussion.

items.example: The revised design is fundamentally different from the prototype.
items.note: Fundamentally signals an essential rather than superficial difference.

items.example: The experimental data flatly contradict the original prediction.
items.note: Flatly adds a strong, unambiguous sense of disagreement or incompatibility.

items.example: The old gate would look better with a lick of paint.
items.note: Informal expression for a small amount or quick application of paint.

items.example: A team of experts reviewed the safety procedure.
items.note: A conventional collective phrase for a group of specialists.

items.example: Her mentor offered a few words of wisdom before the interview.
items.note: Often refers to particularly helpful or insightful advice.

items.example: Could someone come up with a suggestion for reducing delays?
items.note: Come up with means think of and propose something, often a new idea.

items.example: The visitors ran up a substantial bill during their stay.
items.note: Run up commonly combines with bills or debts that accumulate.

items.example: It is difficult to adhere to your principles under intense pressure.
items.note: Adhere to is relatively formal; the object is normally a principle, rule or policy.

items.example: After losing a major contract, the company went on an economy drive.
items.note: A period of deliberate spending cuts; more typical of British English.

items.pt: investir ou especular na bolsa de valores
items.example: He tried to play the stock market without understanding the risks.
items.note: Suggests active market speculation rather than any form of long-term investing.

items.example: She made friends quickly after joining the research group.
items.note: The idiomatic verb is make, not get, for creating friendships.

items.example: Heavy rain forced the organisers to postpone the outdoor session.
items.note: Heavy, rather than strong, is the ordinary adjective with rain.

items.example: Passengers should alight from the bus only at designated stops.
items.note: Alight from is formal, especially in transport notices and instructions.

items.example: We got off the bus near the museum.
items.note: Get off is the everyday alternative to the formal alight from.

items.example: Regular feedback helped the trainees make fewer mistakes.
items.note: The verb is make with mistakes; do mistakes is non-idiomatic.

items.example: Accurate records are of great importance during commissioning.
items.note: Great importance is natural; big importance is not normally used.

items.pt: uma ampla variedade de recursos linguísticos
items.example: The essay demonstrates a wide range of language without sounding artificial.
items.note: Use a wide range of, not a long range of, in this sense.

items.example: For a few hours after the announcement, the whole team was blissfully happy.
items.note: Blissfully suggests carefree, intense happiness.

items.example: They rented a cottage in a picturesque village by the coast.
items.note: Picturesque is common with village, town or landscape.

items.example: The trail offers views of spectacular mountains in every direction.
items.note: Spectacular emphasises striking visual impact.

items.example: Candidates can gain more marks by using precise vocabulary.
items.note: Especially natural in British academic or examination contexts.

items.example: The writer repeated the phrase to create an effect of urgency.
items.note: Create an effect describes an intended impact on readers or audiences.

items.example: Experienced speakers sometimes depart from a familiar pattern for emphasis.
items.note: Depart from is formal and means deviate from an established convention.

items.example: The cabin occupies a secluded location away from the road.
items.note: Secluded suggests privacy and separation from activity.

items.example: The renovated apartment has simple but stylish furnishings.
items.note: Furnishings refers collectively to furniture and other interior fittings.

items.example: The lookout point offers breathtaking views of the valley.
items.note: Breathtaking is strongly positive and often accompanies views.

items.example: Soft music gave the room a relaxing atmosphere.
items.note: Atmosphere describes the general mood or feeling of a place.

items.example: The house has a spacious dining room overlooking the garden.
items.note: Spacious collocates naturally with room and other physical interiors.

items.example: The small café is known for delicious food and friendly service.
items.note: Food is a natural partner for delicious; avoid using good repeatedly.

items.example: Her exhibition contains stunning photographs of the coastline.
items.note: Stunning can describe remarkable images, scenery or performances.

items.pt: culinária de dar água na boca
items.example: The festival introduced visitors to mouth-watering regional cuisine.
items.note: Mouth-watering is especially associated with food and dishes.

items.example: We can grab a bite before heading to the station.
items.note: Informal phrase meaning eat a small or quick meal.

items.example: Once the introductions were over, everyone got down to work.
items.note: Suggests beginning focused work without further delay.

items.word: bring an agreement to an end
items.example: The parties agreed to bring the agreement to an end in December.
items.note: Neutral expression for formally ending an existing arrangement.

items.example: Either organisation may terminate the agreement with written notice.
items.note: Relatively formal, common in contracts and legal documentation.

items.example: He plans to pop the question during their holiday.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning ask someone to marry you.

units.title: Unit 02 — Strong, fixed and weak collocations
learningObjectives: Distinguish strong, fixed and weak collocations with realistic examples.
Use collocations of broad, mitigating, inclement, auburn and deliriously correctly.
Contrast related word partners and account for differences in meaning and register.

items.example: The judge considered several mitigating circumstances before sentencing.
items.note: A legal collocation for circumstances that reduce perceived blame.

items.example: The review panel weighed the mitigating factors carefully.
items.note: Mitigating commonly modifies factors or circumstances.

items.example: The flight was delayed because of inclement weather.
items.note: Rather formal, frequent in notices and announcements.

items.example: Her auburn hair glowed in the afternoon sunlight.
items.note: Auburn describes a reddish-brown shade of hair.

items.example: The young violinist was deliriously happy after her debut.
items.note: Intensifier closely associated with happy, not normally with glad.

items.example: The chair decided to adjourn the meeting until Tuesday.
items.note: Formal meeting vocabulary; use adjourn rather than cancel for a pause.

items.example: The court adjourned the trial after a witness became ill.
items.note: Adjourn is commonly used for temporary suspension of legal proceedings.

items.pt: de um lado para o outro
items.example: The cat wandered to and fro outside the kitchen.
items.note: Fixed expression; the sequence of its words does not vary.

items.pt: em amplo acordo; de modo geral, de acordo
items.example: The two teams were in broad agreement on the objectives.
items.note: Means agreement on main points, without necessarily agreeing on details.

items.example: We cycled along a broad avenue lined with trees.
items.note: Here broad refers to physical width rather than strength or general agreement.

items.example: She greeted the visitors with a broad smile.
items.note: Broad naturally describes the extent of a smile.

items.example: He was recognised by his broad shoulders and distinctive coat.
items.note: Literal use of broad for physical width.

items.example: He speaks English with a broad regional accent.
items.note: Broad may describe a pronounced or distinctive accent.

items.example: Her broad hint about the deadline was hard to miss.
items.note: A broad hint is strongly suggestive rather than subtle.

items.example: We stopped at a picturesque village in the hills.
items.note: Picturesque works with several locations, unlike highly restricted pairs.

items.example: The hotel enjoys a picturesque location beside the lake.
items.note: Describes visually attractive settings, often in promotional language.

items.example: They spent the afternoon exploring a picturesque town.
items.note: A common pairing for places that look charming or visually distinctive.

items.example: She made an effort to speak more clearly in meetings.
items.note: Make is the usual support verb in make an effort.

items.example: Learning the new system may require an effort at first.
items.note: Require an effort highlights the need for deliberate exertion.

items.example: He earns a living as an independent translator.
items.note: A normal expression for obtaining income through work.

items.example: She makes a living by restoring old furniture.
items.note: Equivalent in general sense to earn a living.

items.example: The family scraped a living from a small plot of land.
items.note: Scrape suggests barely earning enough to survive.

items.example: The college had to cancel a class because the lecturer was ill.
items.note: Cancel refers to the event not taking place.

items.example: We had to cancel the meeting at short notice.
items.note: Contrast cancel (not happening) with adjourn (pause or defer).

items.example: The organisers cancelled the match after the storm.
items.note: Used when a scheduled sporting fixture will not take place.

items.example: The supplier tried to cancel the agreement before delivery.
items.note: Use with arrangements or contracts, though terminate is often more formal.

items.example: The courier delivered a letter to the office reception.
items.note: One of several common objects of the verb deliver.

items.example: The inspector delivered a warning about electrical safety.
items.note: Deliver may combine with warnings as well as physical items.

items.pt: realizar o parto de um bebê
items.example: The doctor had to deliver a baby during the storm.
items.note: Medical use: the doctor or midwife assists in childbirth.

items.example: The project manager called a meeting to resolve the issue.
items.note: Call means arrange or convene a meeting, not just telephone.

items.example: The committee will hold a meeting next Wednesday.
items.note: Hold focuses on the meeting taking place.

items.example: A bright light appeared above the control panel.
items.note: Literal use of bright with light.

items.example: They set out early in the bright sunshine.
items.note: A conventional weather combination.

items.example: That is a bright idea for reducing the setup time.
items.note: Figurative sense of bright: clever or promising.

items.example: The young researcher has a bright future ahead.
items.note: Figurative sense of bright: hopeful or promising.

items.pt: envolver-se com uma questão; abordar uma questão
items.example: The report fails to engage with the central issue.
items.note: Means address a topic seriously and directly.

items.example: They engaged the services of a specialist consultant.
items.note: Formal use meaning hire or retain professional help.
